title: Removal of the Automatic Extension of Employment Authorization Documents
summary:
The Department of Homeland Security just ended the practice of automatically extending work permits for most people who file renewal applications on or after October 30, 2025. The change takes effect immediately. If your renewal was filed before that date, your automatic extension still holds, and any extensions provided by law or specific government notices for Temporary Protected Status remain in place. Public comments are open until December 1 on regulations.gov.

DHS says the goal is to complete full security checks and eligibility reviews before granting new work authorization, rather than letting people keep working based on a filing receipt. This reverses a series of policies from 2016–2024 that created and then lengthened automatic extensions (at times up to 540 days) to cushion workers and employers from processing backlogs.

Who could benefit? The government argues the change strengthens public safety and program integrity by ensuring vetting happens first. Employers may also see clearer hiring and reverification steps because an expired card plus a filing receipt will no longer count as proof to keep working. State agencies that issue IDs should face less confusion about documents.

Who might be negatively affected? People waiting on renewals could face gaps in work authorization if their new cards aren’t approved before the old ones expire. That can mean lost income for families and disruption for employers who may need to reassign shifts, hire replacements, or pause services. Small businesses and nonprofits that rely on steady staffing may feel this most. Some individuals also use valid work permits as identity documents, which could be harder to renew on time if processing queues persist.

What to expect next: Filing receipts will clearly state they are not proof of work authorization. Employers must reverify workers by the card’s expiration date. Filing early can help, but if processing delays continue, more people may experience temporary lapses. DHS says it expects fewer filings overall due to other policy changes, which it believes will reduce backlogs over time.
